Why These Roles? EHDS Regulatory Backgro: Why These Roles? EHDS Regulatory Background
The European Health Data Space regulatio: The European Health Data Space regulation establishes a governance framework for both primary use (patient access to their own data) and secondary use (research, innovation, policy-making). Each role in this platform maps to a specific actor defined in the regulation:
Healthcare providers, insurers, and regi: Healthcare providers, insurers, and registries that hold electronic health data are legally required to make it available for authorized secondary use. They retain sovereignty over their data and control access through <o>ODRL policies</o> and contract negotiation.
Researchers, public health agencies, and: Researchers, public health agencies, and innovators who need health data for permitted purposes must apply through an HDAB, receive a data permit, and access data only in a secure processing environment (<s>Art. 73</s>). They never receive raw patient data directly.
Each EU Member State must designate one: Each EU Member State must designate one or more Health Data Access Bodies (HDABs) as the national authority that reviews data access applications, issues data permits, and ensures compliance. MedReg DE represents the German HDAB in this implementation.
The dataspace operator runs the technica: The dataspace operator runs the technical infrastructure: participant onboarding, connector management, federated catalog, and transfer monitoring. They ensure interoperability across all participants but do not access health data directly. No article of the Regulation defines this role; the nearest is the Commission, which operates the central platform of HealthData@EU (Art. 75(8)).
The EHDS gives data users pseudonymised: The EHDS gives data users pseudonymised data only where anonymised data cannot serve the purpose, and keeps the information to reverse the pseudonymisation with the access body or a trusted third party (Art. 66(3)). The secure processing environment keeps identifiable logs of access for at least a year (Art. 73(1)(e)). The Trust Center manages pseudonym resolution and secure processing environment (SPE) sessions, and ensures that data users only access de-identified data.
Navigation is filtered by role: items no: Navigation is filtered by role: items not relevant to a user's function are hidden entirely. This separation of concerns reflects the EHDS principle that each actor should only see the tools and data relevant to their regulatory function.

The Federated button asks every SPE and merges the answers. Every answer about persons is k-anonymous: a count below 5 is shown as <5, and a share computed from it with it.
Example: A researcher asks “What is the: Example: A researcher asks “What is the age distribution?”; the 0-17 group holds one person and comes back as <5, with a k = 5 badge saying how many values were suppressed.
Row-level data is processed only inside: Row-level data is processed only inside a secure processing environment (EHDS Art. 73); only answers leave it. SPE-1 holds AlphaKlinik Berlin's patients, SPE-2 Limburg Medical Centre's, each a Neo4j workspace loaded for the permit, so a federated question has two contributors. Both apply the same rules before anything leaves: the data permit, the ODRL policy, the Art. 71 opt-out (persons who opted out are never counted) and k = 5, including the rule that a contributor with fewer than 5 records withholds the whole answer, since a missing contributor would identify people. Every question is recorded on the audit chain.

Ask a data holder for a contract before: Ask a data holder for a contract before any data moves. Requesting as is the participant you act for. Step 1 lists the providers that offer to it, and Discover Offers fetches their DSP catalog. The offer you select shows its ODRL terms in plain words (what it allows, for how long, on which conditions, what it forbids and what you must do) and the data permits that bind the use as well; once you agree to them on behalf of your participant, Step 2 sends a DSP ContractRequest for that offer. The provider's connector checks the request against its offer and answers on its own: nobody at the provider has to sign in. The page follows the negotiation from REQUESTED to FINALIZED and then offers Continue to transfer; a refused request ends TERMINATED with its reason. The history lists every negotiation of your participant, with a link to the transfer for each agreed one.

Monitor the task queue for pending and a: Monitor the task queue for pending and active data transfer operations. Tasks track the full lifecycle from initiation through provisioning to completion, providing an audit trail for accountability; in the secure processing environment the EHDS requires identifiable access logs (Art. 73(1)(e)).

Each agreed contract appears once, with: Each agreed contract appears once, with where it stands. Start Transfer asks the provider's connector for the data, after the hub has checked that a data permit covers the participant you act as (Art. 61(1)); when none does, the page says whose permit is missing or expired. The page follows the transfer until the data is ready. Open shows the data, Download saves it, and Import into SPE loads it into a secure processing environment (Art. 73); on the live hub a stopped workspace starts first and keeps the data until it stops. The import then closes the transfer, so the access to the provider's data ends; a new transfer imports it again. Details holds the agreed terms, folded until you open them, and every transfer under the contract with its DSP state.

This platform is a <b>reference implemen: This platform is a reference implementation of the European Health Data Space (EHDS) regulation, Regulation (EU) 2025/327. Its purpose is to demonstrate how sovereign health data exchange works in practice, combining the Dataspace Protocol (DSP 2025-1), FHIR R4 clinical resources, OMOP CDM analytics, and biomedical ontologies into a unified Neo4j knowledge graph.

This platform adapts its navigation, persona overview, and available actions to the signed-in user's EHDS role. <b>Verdict.</b> “Verified, key released”: Verdict. “Verified, key released”: the Trustee checked the evidence against its reference values and the data permit's policy hash, and released the key. “Verified, key refused”: the evidence was genuine but did not match, so the workspace holds no data.
<b>Label.</b> “Attested: confidential wo: Label. “Attested: confidential workload” is hardware evidence for this container group, on Azure. “Simulated attestation” means the Trustee, its policy, the key release and the audit record are real, but the evidence comes from the sample attester, so nothing is proven in hardware: this is what the local stack and the static demo show.

: the hardware checks that the workspace runs exactly what the permit allows.
<b>Measurement.</b> The launch measureme: Measurement. The launch measurement of Microsoft's utility VM, which runs the containers. The operator pinned it after comparing it with Microsoft's signed endorsement.
<b>Reported TCB.</b> The firmware versio: Reported TCB. The firmware versions of the host the group runs on. Hosts differ, so the Trustee holds a minimum for each component and accepts any version at or above it: a host with newer AMD firmware passes, one below the minimum is refused.
<b>Key released and Workspace loaded.</b: Key released and Workspace loaded. When the Trustee released the key and when the extract was loaded. The same steps are on the audit chain as spe.attestation, spe.key_release and spe.workspace_loaded, in the tab Secure processing of Audit & Provenance.
<b>Residual trust.</b> The evidence rest: Residual trust. The evidence rests on AMD's root of trust, and the utility VM image is trusted because Microsoft endorses its measurement; the endorsement's issuer and content were checked, its signature not yet cryptographically. The Trustee runs in the hub's own subscription, operated as if by MedReg DE; for the claim to hold fully, the access body runs it in a subscription of its own.
On Azure the workspaces are stopped by d: On Azure the workspaces are stopped by default and start on demand (ADR-072, #774): a federated query or Start on the admin page starts them, which takes about a minute until attestation and key release and three to four minutes until both answer queries; after 30 minutes without a query they stop again. How the attestation is set up, pinned and checked: the runbook. The concepts behind it: the secure processing environment.
